title: The ocean is missing from climate diplomacy. Again.
gist: Bossi argues COP31 in Antalya, Türkiye has no dedicated leaders' event for the ocean among its 15 high-level events (while forests and even glaciers get one), exposing a climate agenda narrowed to electrification and undercutting Australia's promise, as negotiations chair, to elevate Pacific ocean priorities. COP17 in Yerevan likewise found the world off track on 2030 biodiversity targets and produced only another plan.

themes.theme: COP31 agenda hierarchy omits the ocean

insights.claim: None of the 15 listed high-level events at COP31 in Türkiye is explicitly dedicated to the ocean, while forests get dedicated leaders' discussions and financing initiatives and even glaciers get their own high-level event.
insights.speaker: Larelle Bossi
insights.so_what: Ocean/blue-economy finance is unlikely to get headline political commitments at COP31.
insights.quote: Not one of the 15 listed high-level events

insights.claim: COP31's proposed high-level events prioritise electrification, power grids, green industrialisation, finance, forests, waste and methane.
insights.speaker: Larelle Bossi
insights.so_what: Political capital and likely announcements at COP31 cluster around grids, electrification and methane — watch these for policy/finance flows.

insights.claim: What receives leaders' attention, investment and institutional commitment is rarely accidental, so the ocean's absence from the leaders' agenda matters despite its presence in the Action Agenda and pavilions.
insights.speaker: Larelle Bossi
insights.so_what: Leaders'-level placement is a leading indicator of where climate finance will flow.
insights.quote: What receives leaders’ attention, investment and institutional commitment is rarely accidental.

insights.claim: The ocean absorbs more than 90% of the excess heat from global warming and covers more than 70% of the planet, yet lacks a comparable seat at the COP31 table.
insights.speaker: Larelle Bossi
insights.so_what: Underpricing of ocean-climate risk in policy agendas.

insights.claim: Climate action risks being reduced to electrifying the economy; replacing one energy system with another does not resolve ecological and ethical crises such as marine degradation and displacement of coastal communities.
insights.speaker: Larelle Bossi
insights.so_what: Possible future policy pushback against pure-electrification framing; ESG scrutiny of ocean impacts of energy transition (e.g. offshore energy).
insights.quote: have we reduced climate action to electrifying the economy?

insights.claim: A cleaner economy is not necessarily a more just one, nor automatically ecologically sustainable.
insights.speaker: Larelle Bossi
insights.so_what: Just-transition and biodiversity critiques may increasingly shape transition policy.
insights.quote: A cleaner economy is not necessarily a more just one.

insights.claim: The COP17 UN biodiversity summit in Yerevan concluded that the world remains off track to meet its 2030 biodiversity targets, and responded with the Yerevan Pathway, another implementation plan, while financing remains inadequate.
insights.speaker: Larelle Bossi
insights.so_what: Biodiversity finance gap persists; expect more plans than binding money.

insights.claim: COP17 acknowledged the ocean had been overlooked for too long but stopped short of new legally binding commitments.
insights.speaker: Larelle Bossi
insights.so_what: No binding ocean obligations imminent — limited regulatory catalyst for ocean-economy sectors.
insights.locator: There are reasons for cautious optimism

insights.claim: International environmental diplomacy follows a cycle of ambitious targets and celebrated agreements followed by discovering the environment has worsened, prompting yet another plan.
insights.speaker: Larelle Bossi
insights.so_what: Discount headline summit commitments absent funding and enforcement.

insights.claim: The first global assessment under the Kunming–Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework recognises Sustainable Ocean Plans, advanced via the High Level Panel for a Sustainable Ocean Economy, as a way to coordinate fisheries, conservation, tourism, offshore energy and the wider ocean economy.
insights.speaker: Larelle Bossi
entities: High Level Panel for a Sustainable Ocean Economy
insights.so_what: Sustainable Ocean Plans could become the planning framework affecting offshore energy and fisheries siting.

insights.claim: Protecting 30% of the ocean cannot compensate for degrading the remaining 70%, and marine protected areas cannot succeed while fisheries, pollution, development and energy institutions pursue conflicting priorities.
insights.speaker: Larelle Bossi
insights.so_what: 30x30 targets alone won't fix ocean health; cross-sector governance is the bottleneck.
insights.quote: Protecting 30% of the ocean cannot compensate for degrading the remaining 70%.

insights.claim: Australia's COP31 role, including chairing negotiations, came with commitments to elevate Pacific priorities, and elevating the ocean–climate nexus was an explicit priority of the Australia–Pacific COP31 Partnership.
insights.speaker: Larelle Bossi
insights.so_what: Gap between commitment and agenda is a test of Australia's Pacific credibility.

insights.claim: Australia is helping lead a high-level discussion on electrification and supporting a Pacific Resilience Facility pledging event, but neither substitutes for political leadership on the ocean.
insights.speaker: Larelle Bossi
insights.so_what: Pacific Resilience Facility pledges are the concrete Pacific finance deliverable to watch at COP31.
insights.locator: Australia is helping lead a high-level

insights.claim: Pacific leadership should not be reduced to seeking climate-resilience finance; Pacific nations offer an understanding of the ocean as a living system rather than merely a resource.
insights.speaker: Larelle Bossi
insights.so_what: Pacific states may resist being framed purely as aid recipients — relevant to geopolitical competition in the region.
insights.locator: The proposed Pacific Resilience Facility pledging

insights.claim: Without a leaders'-level ocean discussion, the familiar cycle risks repeating: ambitious commitments made in the Pacific are applauded internationally and then quietly diluted when real decisions are made elsewhere.
insights.speaker: Larelle Bossi
insights.so_what: Watch for Pacific disappointment with COP31 outcomes as a regional-diplomacy risk for Australia.
insights.quote: ambitious commitments made in the Pacific, applauded internationally, and quietly diluted when the real political decisions are made elsewhere

top_entities: High Level Panel for a Sustainable Ocean Economy
